payload.unusable_reason: Not a Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal claim: the deceased driver's family claimed against his employers and the vehicle's insurer before the Workmen Compensation Commissioner under workmen's compensation law. The Supreme Court only restored the Commissioner's award; no MACT assessment is involved.

journey.note: Insurer's appeal against the Workmen Compensation Commissioner's award of Rs 4,27,148 with 12% interest. The High Court set the award aside and sent the case back to decide whether the deceased was the policy-holder owner's employee. The Commissioner is not a MACT, so no tribunal step is recorded.

Widow's appeal allowed: the remand was unnecessary because the insurer is liable whether or not the vehicle had been sold. The Commissioner's Rs 4,27,148 with 12% interest from the date of the accident was restored.

extraction.title_anon: Man, 26, employed driver, Uttar Pradesh (death, workmen's compensation)
extraction.family_summary: A 26-year-old driver earning Rs 4,000 a month died on the spot in September 2003 when a truck hit the vehicle he was driving. His father claimed under workmen's compensation law, not before a motor accident claims tribunal, and the Commissioner awarded Rs 4,27,148 with 12% interest. In December 2014 the High Court set this aside on the insurer's appeal and sent the case back. On his widow's appeal in July 2017, almost 14 years after the accident, the Supreme Court restored the Rs 4,27,148 with 12% interest from the date of the accident.
what_mattered: The insurer stayed liable whether or not the vehicle had been sold: following Rikhi Ram and Section 157 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the policy passes to a buyer along with the vehicle, so the sale does not end the insurer's liability to third parties.

The owner named on the policy never produced the registration certificate or any proof of the sale, so the Commissioner was right to treat him as still the owner, and the High Court's remand to decide who employed the driver was unnecessary.
